chunks: Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, from al-Faḍl ibn Shādhān and ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, all together from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥafṣ ibn al-Bakhtarī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

Indeed, Jibrāʾīl عليه السلام dug five rivers with his foot, and the tongue of the water followed him: the Euphrates, the Tigris, the Nile of Egypt, Mihrān, and the river of Balkh. So whatever they water, or whatever is watered from them, belongs to the Imam, and the sea surrounding the world belongs to the Imam.

key_terms.الْإِمَامِ: the Imam, to whom these watered domains are said to belong
key_terms.جَبْرَئِيلَ: Jibrāʾīl عليه السلام, the angel mentioned as the one who dug the rivers
key_terms.خَمْسَةَ أَنْهَارٍ: five rivers specifically named in the narration
key_terms.لِسَانُ الْمَاءِ: the flow or leading extension of the water that followed

ai.seo_question: How does al-Kāfī describe the Imam’s authority over major rivers and the seas of the world?
ai.summary: This hadith attributes the emergence of five major rivers to Jibrāʾīl عليه السلام and states that what is irrigated by them belongs to the Imam. It also affirms that the sea encompassing the world is for the Imam, expressing the Imam’s divinely designated authority over the earth’s major natural domains and resources.

en.hubeali:
Muhammad Bin Ismail, from Al Fazl Bin Shazan and Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, altogether from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Hafs Bin Al Bakhtary, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘Jibraeel<sup>as</sup> dug five rivers by his<sup>as</sup> leg and the strip of the water followed it – The Euphrates, and Dajla, and Nile of Egypt, and Mihran, and river Balkh. So whatever is watered or drawn from these, so it is for the Imam<sup>asws</sup>, and the oceans circling the earth are for the Imam<sup>asws</sup>’.
en.sarwar: Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from al-Sarriy ibn al-Rabi‘ who has said the following. “Ibn abu ’Umayr would not consider anyone a match of Hisham ibn al-Hakam in anything. He would not miss meeting him. However, their relations at a time stood at a distance. The reason for this was the emrgence of diffirences between ibn abu ‘Umayr and and abu Malik al-Hadrami, a friend of Hisham, over the issue of Imamat. Ibn abu ‘Umayr had said that the whole world belongs to the Imam in the form of property and ownership and that he has more authority over it than those who have certain parts of it in their possession.

Abu Malik had said that it is not as suCh The peoples properties belong to them except what Allah has given to the Imam in the form of windfall profits and one fifth taxes or interests. Such properties belong to the Imam and Allah has instructed him how to spent them and what to do with them. They agreed to ask Hisham to settle the differences. They went to Hisham but he supported the idea of abu Malik. Ibn abu ‘Umayr became angry and distanced himself from Hisham thereafter.”
